summary: This is a Docusaurus plugin that generates RSS feeds for blog posts. It creates a main site-wide feed plus optional per-tag and per-series feeds, extracting article content from built HTML files, cleaning out UI elements, and injecting author metadata. The plugin respects front matter flags like draft status, handles multi-language sites carefully, and converts relative URLs to absolute ones so feed readers can access linked images and pages.

explanations.70: This utility joins URL path segments using forward slashes (POSIX style) and ensures the result always starts with a slash, since RSS feed URLs need that format.
explanations.82: This combines a website's base domain (siteUrl), its path prefix (baseUrl), and a relative path into one complete URL — for example, turning 'example.com', '/docs/', and 'blog/post' into 'example.com/docs/blog/post'.
explanations.94: This looks at the file extension of an image URL and returns the appropriate MIME type string that RSS readers expect, like 'image/jpeg' or 'image/webp'.
explanations.119: This removes invisible or control characters that would break XML parsers — things like zero-width spaces, non-breaking spaces, and unprintable control codes.
explanations.143: This combines three layers of CSS selectors to remove: always-strip ones (header, svg), defaults built into the plugin, and user-provided ones, so nothing gets duplicated.
explanations.158: When a post is at `/fr/blog/post` and we naively join that with `build/fr/`, we'd get `build/fr/fr/blog/post` (doubled locale). This function detects and strips that duplicate prefix so we look in the right place.
explanations.177: This tries to find the article's main content container using a chain of fallbacks: first look for an `<article>` tag, then theme-specific divs, giving us flexibility across different Docusaurus setups.
explanations.188: For each CSS selector in our removal list, this finds all matching elements inside the article and deletes them — for example, removing related-posts sections or comment placeholders.
explanations.193: Docusaurus wraps code snippets in a custom container. This unwraps them by replacing the outer wrapper with just the actual code block, giving cleaner RSS content.
explanations.210: This computes the URL slug (the 'post' part of '/blog/post') from front matter if set, otherwise derives it from the filename, handling special cases like `folder/index.md`.
explanations.278: Instead of using today's date as the feed's last-update time, we use the newest post's date. This prevents the entire feed file from rewriting on every build when nothing changed, saving deploy bandwidth.
explanations.291: Blog posts can have one author or multiple authors listed in front matter (as a single key or an array). This normalizes it to always be an array so the next lines work uniformly.
explanations.318: If a post's front matter has an image URL, we convert it to an absolute URL using the site domain and base path, since RSS readers need the full URL to fetch it.
explanations.324: We start with just the description text, but if image inclusion is enabled, we prepend an `` tag pointing to that absolute image URL, so RSS readers show a thumbnail.
explanations.367: We load the already-serialized RSS XML back into Cheerio (in XML mode) so we can surgically insert `<dc:creator>` tags after generation, since the RSS library doesn't natively support them.
explanations.370: We add the Dublin Core namespace declaration to the root `<rss>` element so XML parsers know that 'dc:' prefixed tags like `<dc:creator>` are valid.
explanations.383: We walk through each `<item>` in the feed and inject its corresponding author markup at that position. Order matters because arrays are matched by index: first item gets first creator markup, etc.
explanations.395: We replace the default XML declaration with one that also references an XSL stylesheet for pretty-printing, using an absolute path so it works for feeds at any depth.
explanations.424: We import the `feed` npm package dynamically here instead of at the top, allowing it to be an optional dependency that users only need if they use this plugin.
explanations.449: We load a YAML file listing author definitions (name, bio, etc.) keyed by ID, then use it later to look up full author details when a post references author IDs.
explanations.462: This finds all Markdown/MDX files in the blog directory, excluding any matching the ignore patterns (like archived posts), so we know which posts to process.
explanations.478: Posts marked as draft or unlisted in front matter never get an HTML page built, so they can't have RSS content extracted. We skip them early to avoid fruitless file-not-found errors.
explanations.482: We grab the publication date from front matter if set, otherwise fall back to the file's creation time (birthtime), giving us a date for sorting.
explanations.509: For each post's metadata, we now fetch its actual built HTML file, parse it with Cheerio, strip out unwanted elements, and extract just the article body for the RSS feed.
explanations.521: We filter to only include posts marked as published and that actually have content, then sort newest first, so the RSS feed lists recent posts at the top.
explanations.530: For non-default locales (like French), we check which posts are actually translated. Without this, Docusaurus's i18n fallback would let English posts masquerade as French content in the French feed.
explanations.550: We take only the first N items (up to maxItems) from the sorted published posts, ensuring the final feed doesn't balloon in size.
explanations.601: This groups posts by their tags (for example, grouping all 'javascript' posts together) using a helper function, then loops through each group to build a separate feed.
explanations.610: We skip tag feeds with fewer posts than minPostsPerTagFeed, preventing tiny one-item feeds. This is normally 1 (so every tag gets a feed), but can be raised to enforce a minimum.
explanations.628: Similar to tags, we group posts by series (if they belong to a multi-part sequence), then create a feed for each series so readers can follow just that story arc.
explanations.649: Each topic feed is capped at topicMaxItems (default 10, vs. 20 for the main feed), keeping per-topic feeds smaller since they're one of many copies.
explanations.660: Topic feeds omit the full article body (includeContent: false) to save space, since the reader's job is to discover posts and click through, not read everything in the feed.
